The assignment criteria, re-checked against each paper

Prof. von Maydell's rubric demands: (1) full paper, ≥8 pages; (2) from ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, or Google Scholar; (3) you can explain why it's important for the course and how it tackles GenAI and creativity; (4) you can state where and by whom it was published. Let me score each honestly.

Casacuberta & Guersenzvaig — 9 pages, Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence (August 2025), by two design philosophers at Universitat Autònoma Barcelona and Elisava. Journal paper, not SIGCHI — but findable on Google Scholar, which is one of the three allowed sources. This matters: the assignment slide says "ACM DL, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore" — it doesn't restrict you to SIGCHI. You can legitimately defend this choice. It meets every criterion.

Protosampling (Guo et al.) — arXiv preprint from January 2026, Autodesk Research. Not yet in ACM DL as of now. This is a risk. It's 26 pages, so length isn't the issue — the issue is it's not yet peer-reviewed at a SIGCHI venue. If Prof. von Maydell asks "where was it published?", you'd have to say "arXiv preprint, likely heading to CHI or C&C 2026." That's a weaker answer.

Designing Interactions Taxonomy (Hu et al.) — DIS 2025, 30 pages, SIGCHI venue. Meets every criterion perfectly on paper. But — and this is important — it's a systematic review, not a primary research paper. You'd be presenting "a paper that reviews 189 other papers." That's meta-level, one step removed from your actual argument.

Productive vs. Reflective (Xu et al.) — CHI 2025, 15 pages, SIGCHI venue, UCSD. Perfect on rubric. Strong empirical study. But here's the thing: its main finding is about how interface placement of AI scaffolding affects cognitive engagement in design-thinking templates. That's genuinely adjacent to your argument, but it's not the argument itself.

The deeper question: which paper is actually about what you believe?

This is where the decision gets clear. You wrote 13 pages in a notebook arguing two things:

Heavy AI reliance is quietly eroding human skill — specifically through the prompt-as-interface model that prevents embodied engagement with the creative medium.

Visual creative tools built around text prompts are fundamentally wrong-designed for a visual medium; canvas-based tools would be better.

Now let me show you what each paper actually argues:

Casacuberta & Guersenzvaig argues: Prompt-based GenAI disembodies creativity, sequesters users in novice-level engagement, and cannot develop expert skill because prompting cannot externalize tacit knowledge. Every tool affords some directions but not others — pencils can't carve marble — and prompt-text cannot afford what visual creative work needs. This is your notebook. Written by philosophers. With proper academic references to Dreyfus, Polanyi, Sennett, Pallasmaa — the names that give your intuitions philosophical weight.

Protosampling argues: Current GenAI interfaces sit on a spectrum from simple chat to complex node-based programming, leaving a gap for creative practitioners; we built Atelier, a canvas-based system that tightens sampling and prototyping into a joint activity. This is your solution — literally a paper proposing the canvas-based video/image tool you said you want to build. It's the tool side of your argument.

Designing Interactions Taxonomy argues: Creative GenAI systems fall into four paradigms — medium, tool, partner, mediator — and most of the field is still inductively experimenting without clear framing. This is the map of the design space your future startup would navigate.

Productive vs. Reflective argues: The way AI support is positioned in design workflows (No-AI, Co-led, AI-led) changes the cognition: AI-led participants offload synthesis, while Co-led participants retain more agency and critical engagement. This is empirical evidence that interface framing changes thinking — adjacent to your argument but not the argument itself.

Why Casacuberta & Guersenzvaig is the right Monday paper

Three reasons, in increasing importance.

First — it's the cleanest match to your verbal intro requirements. The three things Prof. von Maydell asked you to prepare are: (1) why is it important for the course, (2) what is it about, (3) where was it published. For this paper, every answer is crisp. (1) Because it critiques the dominant GenAI creativity paradigm — prompting — on philosophical grounds that the HCI literature hasn't fully articulated; it reframes "democratization" as "novice-entrapment." (2) It argues prompt-based GenAI creates a new, disembodied mode of creation that bypasses skill acquisition and embodied engagement, and that this mode is ontologically distinct from human creative practice. (3) Frontiers in AI, August 2025, by David Casacuberta and Ariel Guersenzvaig, design philosophers at UAB and Elisava School of Design. Clean, three sentences, done.

Second — it gives you intellectual scaffolding the others don't. The other three papers describe what's happening (taxonomy, experiment, system). Casacuberta & Guersenzvaig tell you why it matters philosophically. They introduce vocabulary you can reuse across your whole semester: disembodied creativity, tacit knowledge, the five-stage Dreyfus skill model, "midtended" agency, the distinction between being-inspired-by versus creating-with, first-person embodied loops between mind-hand-surroundings. These are the concepts that will make your longer presentation sound like a seminar talk rather than a student assignment. Walking in with this paper Monday primes the whole semester.

Third — and this is the real reason — it matches the version of yourself you want to be in class. You are not an HCI engineer building creative tools. You are a student with strong instincts about where AI is going wrong, wanting to articulate a position. A paper by two philosophers who take that position seriously gives you permission to speak as a thinker, not just a systems reviewer. When Prof. von Maydell asks "why this paper?" — your honest answer is "because it says what I've been trying to say, and it says it in the vocabulary of design philosophy." That's a much more compelling intro than "this paper reports on a controlled study of 47 participants."

The pros and cons, laid flat

Casacuberta & Guersenzvaig (pick this)
Pros: perfect thesis alignment, philosophical depth, open access, crisp length (9 pages), introduces vocabulary you'll reuse all semester, published August 2025 (genuinely recent), defensible via Google Scholar as source.
Cons: journal not SIGCHI — if Prof. von Maydell interprets the rubric as "conference only," you'd need to defend the choice. Not an empirical study, so you can't cite "findings" in the traditional sense. Dense philosophical references (Dreyfus, Polanyi, Pallasmaa) — you'll need to be ready if asked to explain them.

Protosampling (Guo et al.)
Pros: literally describes the tool you said you want to build — canvas-based visual AI for filmmaking, including storyboarding a warrior-and-dragon film sequence. 5-participant user study with film professionals. Directly addresses your canvas-vs-prompt critique with a working system.
Cons: arXiv preprint as of January 2026, not yet peer-reviewed at a SIGCHI venue. System-paper, so you'd spend most of your verbal intro describing what Atelier is rather than what position the paper takes. It's a better paper for your longer presentation than for this 3-sentence intro.

Designing Interactions Taxonomy (Hu et al.)
Pros: SIGCHI-sponsored DIS 2025, perfect rubric fit. 189 papers reviewed, four-paradigm taxonomy (medium/tool/partner/mediator), confirms empirically that canvas interfaces dominate visual creative work. Perfect structural backbone for your longer presentation.
Cons: it's a systematic review of other people's work — you'd be presenting a paper about papers. The verbal intro gets awkward: "this paper is important because it reviews the field." That's true but doesn't foreground your position. Save this one for the longer presentation where taxonomy genuinely helps structure your argument.

Productive vs. Reflective (Xu et al.)
Pros: SIGCHI CHI 2025, perfect rubric, rigorous experiment (47 participants, three conditions), direct empirical evidence that interface framing changes cognitive engagement. Great paper.
Cons: about design-thinking templates and collaborative whiteboard plugins, not about filmmaking or canvas-based visual tools. Its argument is interface-framing-matters, which is adjacent to yours but in a different domain. The fit is good, not perfect.

My recommendation, stated once, clearly

Go with Casacuberta & Guersenzvaig for Monday.

It is the paper closest to what you actually believe. It gives you a philosophical vocabulary the course has not yet heard. It is short enough (9 pages) to read carefully tonight and genuinely absorb, not just skim. And the concepts it introduces — disembodied creativity, tacit knowledge, Dreyfus stages, midtended agency — will transfer directly into your longer presentation lineup where you can then pair it with Protosampling (as the design response to the problem this paper diagnoses) and the Taxonomy paper (as the map of the design space).

If Prof. von Maydell challenges you on it not being SIGCHI: the assignment slide lists Google Scholar as one of three acceptable sources. This paper is on Google Scholar. It is peer-reviewed (Frontiers in AI, reviewed by Lorenzo Magnani at Pavia, Woosuk Park at KAIST, Atocha Aliseda at UNAM — serious philosophers of AI). You can defend the choice calmly.

Your three-sentence verbal intro, ready to memorize:

"I picked Disembodied Creativity in Generative AI by Casacuberta and Guersenzvaig, published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence in August 2025. They argue that prompt-based GenAI creates a fundamentally different kind of creativity than human creative practice — one that is disembodied, rule-based, and keeps users stuck at novice-level engagement, because tacit craft knowledge can't be externalized into text prompts. I chose it because it gives philosophical grounding to a concern I've had about my own practice: that AI filmmaking tools built around text prompts might be making us more productive while quietly eroding the visual and embodied skills we were supposed to develop."

That's it. That's your opening on Monday.

For the longer presentation proposal, carry Protosampling and the Taxonomy paper as your other two anchors. Casacuberta diagnoses the problem, Protosampling proposes the canvas-based response, the Taxonomy maps the four paradigms your future startup must choose between. Three papers, one argument, every citation defensible.

Read the Casacuberta paper tonight — abstract and introduction carefully, then sections 2.1 and 2.2 on embodiment and the five-stage Dreyfus model. That's the core. Print it. Sleep on it. You'll walk in Monday with the clearest thesis in the room.
